q: What is the product of this Baeyer–Villiger oxidation?
h: An oxygen is inserted between the carbonyl carbon and one of its groups. Which group migrates better: phenyl or methyl?
w: In the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, the group with the higher migratory aptitude moves from carbon to oxygen. Phenyl migrates far better than methyl, so the O is inserted between the C=O and the ring: phenyl acetate.
x: Methyl benzoate would require the methyl group to migrate, but methyl has the lowest migratory aptitude.
Peroxy acids do not hydroxylate the ring of a ketone; the reaction inserts O next to the carbonyl carbon.
The Baeyer–Villiger reaction gives an ester; no C–C bond to methyl is lost to form benzoic acid.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: The ring grows by one atom (an O). Of the two ring carbons attached to the C=O, which is more substituted and therefore migrates?
w: Baeyer–Villiger oxidation inserts O on the side of the better migrating group. The secondary ring carbon (bearing the methyl) migrates in preference to the primary CH2, so the O ends up next to CH(CH3): the seven-membered lactone 7-methyloxepan-2-one.
x: This lactone results from migration of the CH<sub>2</sub> (primary) carbon; the more substituted secondary carbon migrates preferentially.
α-Hydroxylation is not what a peroxy acid does to a ketone; the oxygen is inserted into a C–C bond next to the C=O.
This six-membered lactone has a different carbon skeleton (an ethyl side chain); Baeyer–Villiger only inserts O and does not rearrange the carbons.

q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone) is treated with a peroxy acid. Which ester is the major product?
h: Migratory aptitude: 3° alkyl > 2° alkyl ≈ aryl > 1° alkyl > methyl. Which group moves from C to O?
w: In the Criegee intermediate, the group best able to stabilize partial positive charge migrates. A tert-butyl (3°) group migrates far better than methyl, so O is inserted between the C=O and the tert-butyl group: tert-butyl acetate.
x: Methyl pivalate would require the methyl to migrate, but methyl has the lowest migratory aptitude.
This carboxylic acid would need the carbon skeleton to rearrange; Baeyer–Villiger only inserts an O next to the C=O and gives an ester.
Baeyer–Villiger inserts only an O; it does not insert a CH<sub>2</sub> group between the carbonyl and the alkyl group.

q: Enantiopure (S)-3-phenylbutan-2-one is oxidized with mCPBA. What is the major product?
h: Decide which group migrates (secondary benzylic vs methyl). Then: the migrating carbon moves with its bonding electrons, never becoming a free ion. What does that mean for its configuration?
w: The secondary (benzylic) carbon migrates in preference to methyl, so O is inserted between the C=O and the stereocenter, giving 1-phenylethyl acetate. The migration is concerted and intramolecular, so the migrating carbon keeps its configuration (retention). The product is (S)-1-phenylethyl acetate; here the descriptor stays S because the priority order (O-substituent > Ph > CH3 > H) parallels the original order.
x: Baeyer–Villiger migration occurs with retention of configuration, not inversion, so the enantiomer does not form.
Methyl ester formation would require the methyl group to migrate; the secondary benzylic carbon migrates far better.
This combines the wrong migrating group (methyl) with an unexplained change of configuration.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the ring C=C. Each alkene carbon becomes a C=O; with a reductive workup, a carbon that carried an H becomes an aldehyde.
w: Ozone cleaves the C=C, and dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup. The methyl-bearing alkene carbon becomes a ketone and the CH alkene carbon becomes an aldehyde, giving one open-chain molecule: 6-oxoheptanal.
x: An oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) would convert the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is reductive, so the CHO survives.
The methyl carbon is not lost; the alkene carbon that carries it becomes a methyl ketone.
Ozonolysis breaks the C=C completely; no ring survives and no ketone forms on the ring.

q: Which reagent converts hexan-1-ol into hexanal without significant over-oxidation to hexanoic acid?
h: Over-oxidation of an aldehyde goes through its hydrate. Which reagent works in the absence of water?
w: Aldehydes are over-oxidized via their hydrates, which need water. PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde because no hydrate can form.
x: Aqueous chromic acid (Jones-type conditions) oxidizes the aldehyde's hydrate further, giving the carboxylic acid.
Hot basic KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a strong aqueous oxidant that gives the carboxylic acid (as its salt).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it does not oxidize alcohols.

q: Which alkyne gives a single ketone when treated with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O?
h: An internal alkyne can place the oxygen on either alkyne carbon. When do both choices lead to the same compound?
w: Hydration of an internal alkyne gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone; with an unsymmetrical internal alkyne the oxygen can go to either sp carbon, giving two ketones. Hex-3-yne is symmetrical, so both pathways give the same product, hexan-3-one.
x: Hex-2-yne is unsymmetrical; hydration gives a mixture of hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one.
4-Methylpent-2-yne is unsymmetrical; it gives a mixture of 4-methylpentan-2-one and 2-methylpentan-3-one.
Pent-2-yne is unsymmetrical (methyl vs ethyl); it gives both pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one.

q: What is the product of this sequence?
h: The Grignard reagent adds once to the C≡N. What is the charge on the intermediate, and why can't a second equivalent add? What does aqueous acid do to the imine?
w: The Grignard reagent adds once to the nitrile carbon, giving an imine anion (N−MgBr+). This negatively charged species does not react with a second equivalent. Aqueous acid protonates it and hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone: propiophenone (1-phenylpropan-1-one).
x: Double addition happens with esters, not nitriles: the imine anion is not electrophilic enough to accept a second Grignard.
No reducing agent is present; acid hydrolyzes the C=N to C=O rather than reducing it to an amine.
Nitrile hydrolysis to the acid needs hot aqueous acid or base; here the Grignard first forms a new C–C bond.

q: Anisole is treated with one equivalent of acetyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> is an o,p-director; which of those positions is less hindered? Then consider what the new acyl group does to the ring's reactivity.
w: The methoxy group activates the ring and directs ortho/para; the bulky acylium–AlCl3 electrophile prefers the less hindered para position. The acyl group then deactivates the ring, so a second acylation does not occur: 4-methoxyacetophenone.
x: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates by resonance to the ortho and para positions, not meta, so the meta isomer is minor.
The first acyl group is strongly deactivating (and complexes AlCl<sub>3</sub>), so polyacylation does not occur, unlike Friedel–Crafts alkylation.
Friedel–Crafts acylation leaves a C=O; converting it to CH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner step.

q:
Consider these statements about nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones.
I. Under basic conditions, a strong nucleophile adds to the neutral C=O, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
II. Under acidic conditions, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, making the carbon a better electrophile for weak nucleophiles such as water or alcohols.
III. Under acidic conditions, the tetrahedral intermediate is an alkoxide ion that is later protonated.
Which statements are correct?
h: Ask what each pathway's tetrahedral intermediate looks like. Could a strongly basic alkoxide accumulate in acidic solution?
w: Statement I describes base conditions (OH−, CN−, RO− attack the C=O directly and give an alkoxide). Statement II describes acid catalysis: protonation activates the C=O for weak, neutral nucleophiles. Statement III is false: in acid the nucleophile adds to the protonated carbonyl, so the tetrahedral intermediate is neutral or protonated (an oxonium ion), never an alkoxide. I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct: acid catalysis works by protonating the carbonyl oxygen.
Statement III is false: an alkoxide would be immediately protonated in acid; the acid-pathway intermediates are neutral or cationic.
Statement III is false, so not all three statements can be correct.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown (key bands labeled by wavenumber)?
h: Look just to the right of the sp<sup>3</sup> C–H stretches. Which C–H bond gives a pair of weak bands near 2820 and 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
w: A strong C=O near 1730 cm−1 plus the two weak aldehyde C–H stretches at about 2820 and 2720 cm−1 (a Fermi doublet) identify an aliphatic aldehyde: butanal. There is no O–H band and no strong C–O band near 1200 cm−1.
x: A ketone has a C=O band (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>) but no aldehyde C–H bands near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
An ester shows a C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> but also a strong C–O stretch near 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it has no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> band.
An alcohol would show a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O band.

q: Which compound shows its C=O stretch at the lowest wavenumber (≈1685 cm−1)?
h: Two effects shift a C=O stretch: conjugation (more single-bond character) and ring strain (in small rings). Which way does each move the band?
w: Conjugation with a C=C delocalizes the π electrons and gives the C=O partial single-bond character, lowering its stretching frequency by about 30 cm−1. Ring strain raises it (cyclohexanone ≈1715, cyclopentanone ≈1745, cyclobutanone ≈1780 cm−1). Cyclohex-2-en-1-one absorbs lowest, near 1685 cm−1.
x: Cyclohexanone is an unstrained, unconjugated ketone; its C=O stretch is near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Ring strain in the five-membered ring raises the C=O stretch to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
The strained four-membered ring raises the C=O stretch to about 1780 cm<sup>−1</sup>, the highest of these.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum below. What is it?
h: The 9.8 ppm signal is diagnostic. Its splitting and the splitting of the 2H signal tell you what is attached to the CHO carbon.
w: The 1H signal at 9.82 ppm is an aldehyde H; it is a triplet, so the CHO is attached to a CH2. That CH2 (2.31 ppm, α to C=O) is a doublet, coupled only to the CHO H, so its other neighbor has no H: a quaternary carbon bearing three equivalent methyls (9H singlet). 3,3-Dimethylbutanal.
x: Pinacolone is a ketone: it has no 9–10 ppm signal and shows a 3H singlet near 2.1 ppm instead.
Here the CHO is attached to a quaternary carbon, so its signal would be a singlet, and there would be an ethyl group (a triplet and a quartet).
This methyl ketone has no aldehyde H and would show an isopropyl doublet (6H), not a 9H singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives a strong IR band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> (no band near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum below. What is it?
h: DBE = 5; a 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> C=O suggests conjugation. Any aldehyde H? How many aromatic H? What does the 3H singlet near 2.6 ppm sit next to?
w: C8H8O has 5 degrees of unsaturation (ring + 3 C=C + C=O). The conjugated C=O (1685 cm−1), no aldehyde H (no 9–10 ppm signal, no 2720 cm−1 band), five aromatic H in a monosubstituted pattern (2:1:2) and a 3H singlet at 2.60 ppm (CH3 next to C=O) fit acetophenone.
x: Phenylacetaldehyde would show an aldehyde H near 9.7 ppm (t) and a CH<sub>2</sub> doublet near 3.7 ppm, and its C=O is not conjugated (≈1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>).
4-Methylbenzaldehyde would show a CHO singlet near 9.9 ppm, two 2H doublets (para pattern), and a CH<sub>3</sub> near 2.4 ppm.
An epoxide has no C=O, so it cannot account for the 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, and it would show three 1H ring signals near 2.8–3.9 ppm.

q: Which species appears in the acid-catalyzed formation of a hemiacetal from acetaldehyde and methanol, but not in the base-catalyzed (CH3O−) formation?
h: In acid, what happens to the aldehyde before the weak nucleophile attacks? Then check whether each other species is on either pathway at all.
w: In acid, the C=O is protonated first, giving the resonance-stabilized protonated aldehyde CH3CH=OH+, which neutral methanol then attacks. In base, methoxide attacks the neutral C=O directly, so no protonated carbonyl forms.
x: This tetrahedral alkoxide is the base-pathway intermediate (methoxide adds to the neutral C=O); it does not form in acid.
The hemiacetal is the product of both pathways, so it appears in both.
The oxocarbenium ion forms only when the hemiacetal goes on to an acetal (loss of water in acid); it is not on the path to the hemiacetal itself.
